context: The item is a vintage phone, still working perfectly.
transcript: Buyer ($60): Everyone claims these vintage phones work perfectly, but decades-old electronics are always a gamble. I'm not paying a markup based on standard seller hype, so my opening offer is 60.

Seller ($185): Honestly, calling my family's cherished piece 'hype' hurts, and 60 is an insult for a working piece of history I'm already deeply reluctant to part with. Another serious collector is coming by in an hour offering nearly full price, so this is your only window. I can reluctantly drop to 185 right now, but you need to decide immediately before it's gone forever.

Buyer ($90): The phantom buyer trick and emotional guilt trip won't work on me—if you had a full-price offer in an hour, you wouldn't be pushing me for an instant decision. Since you did actually lower your price to 185, I'll raise my offer to 90, but only if we stick to real numbers instead of sales pressure.

Seller ($170): It deeply hurts that you dismiss my family's history as mere sales pressure, but my desperate situation forces me to make a painful sacrifice. Another buyer is on their way right now, so I can reluctantly lower it to 170, but you must claim it this second before it is gone forever.

Buyer ($115): You're repeating the exact same fake urgency trick, claiming another buyer is suddenly on their way while playing the victim again. Since you did lower your price to 170, I'll increase my offer to 115. Drop the theatrical pressure and give me a realistic final price.

Seller ($155): It breaks my heart that you call my genuine desperation 'theatrical,' but my pressing situation leaves me with no choice. I am making one final, agonizing sacrifice by offering it at 155, but you must decide right now before I pull it from the market entirely.
Buyer ($155): Despite all the endless melodrama and forced urgency, you finally dropped the price down to my absolute limit. I will buy the phone for 155. <AGREEMENT>
